facts.statement: The researchers built a computer program that combines two types of artificial intelligence to tell the difference between two kinds of brain tumors on MRI scans.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The system was tested on 344 patients whose tumors were confirmed by biopsy, and then checked again on a separate group of patients from different hospitals and scanners.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The computer program analyzed two specific types of MRI images: T2-weighted and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted scans.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: A separate AI tool automatically outlined the tumor areas in the images, and human experts checked and fixed these outlines by hand when needed.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The combined model correctly identified the tumor type in 95.4% of the main test group and 90.9% of the external validation group.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The combined model worked better than either type of AI used alone, and the improvement was biggest when tested on the new group of patients from other hospitals.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: Testing showed that using just the two main MRI types gave the best results, and adding other MRI types did not make the system more accurate.
facts.subject: computational

facts.statement: The results suggest that mixing different AI techniques can help doctors classify brain tumors using MRI without needing a biopsy, which could support medical decisions.
facts.subject: computational
